{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.","text":"On the edge of a quiet harbor stood a blue wooden boat that no one had sailed in years. Its name, painted in white letters along the bow, was Morning Star. Each day, old Mr. Bell swept the deck and polished the brass bell, though he never explained why he kept the boat ready.

One spring morning, a storm pushed a small rowboat against the harbor wall. A young sailor climbed out, soaked and shivering. He had lost his way in the fog and damaged his oars on the rocks.

Mr. Bell welcomed him into the boathouse and made a pot of tea. As the sailor warmed his hands, he noticed a faded photograph on the wall. It showed a woman at the helm of the Morning Star, laughing into the wind.

“That was my daughter, Anna,” Mr. Bell said. “She used to take this boat beyond the headland. She taught me that the sea is less frightening when you know someone is waiting on shore.”

The sailor asked if the boat still worked. Mr. Bell looked across the harbor, where sunlight was beginning to break through the clouds. Together, they checked the sails, tightened a loose rope, and filled the water tank.

By noon, the Morning Star was gliding out of the harbor. Mr. Bell stood at the pier, holding the brass bell. For the first time in many years, he rang it—not as a goodbye, but as a promise.

When the boat returned at sunset, the sailor carried a fresh photograph. Mr. Bell placed it beside Anna’s, then began polishing the bell again."}
